newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria coalition lives but with health impaired.
newsitem.headline: Austria coalition lives but with health impaired.

text.p: Austria's two-party government scraped through an almost fatal clash over bank privatisation at the weekend but symptoms of a deeper malaise have gripped a coalition that may not survive long, analysts said on Monday.

The coalition of Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats and Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel's conservatives ended weeks of turmoil on Sunday by agreeing that the country's biggest bank, Bank Austria, should be allowed to buy second-ranking bank Creditanstalt-Bankverein.

But political observers were almost unanimous that Schuessel's party was the overall loser in the deal by relinquishing its influence over Creditanstalt to Bank Austria and its patrons, the Social Democrats.

"It's almost impossible for this coalition to continue functioning properly. The probability of a government breakdown has increased," said Andreas Unterberger, editor of Die Presse daily. "Bank Austria will remain under the influence of the Social Democrats."

"I can't believe the majority of conservatives are really satisfied with the decision because they have definitely lost their bank within the Austrian economy," said analyst Alfred Reisenberger at brokerage IMI Group Sigeco in London.

Observers say continual bickering between the two parties hands political capital to far-right leader Joerg Haider. A year-old Social Democrat-conservative coalition broke down in October 1995 in a row over cutting the budget.
Haider said on Sunday that his nationalist Freedom Party was poised to enter government as the bank selloff proved the two parties could no longer rule the country effectively.
Haider's anti-immigration party won nearly 28 percent of the vote in European elections last October, just a few thousand votes behind the two main parties.

Polls showed that the far right captured nearly 50 percent of traditional Social Democrat working class support in October and Haider is intent on pulling in support from conservative voters, such as the large number of farmers disillusioned over European Union membership.

Haider jibes at the conservatives, telling them they are being constantly humiliated by Vranitzky's party and if they want to hold on to any real power they should consider linking up with the Freedom Party in a future coalition.

A further cause of strife down the road may be the security of bank jobs. Senior conservatives stressed on Monday they had won guarantees for Creditanstalt workers but analysts said it was those very workers who may bear the brunt in the future.
"Bank Austria...has tight labour contracts so a lot of job cuts will have to come from Creditanstalt and that won't be popular," said analyst Victoria Maxwell of James Capel, London.

Austria's post-1945 consensus politics has been governed by an unwritten rule, assuring a shareout of all the top jobs in the economy, state-controlled industry and other institutions to the two main parties. This system is breaking down, and Schuessel's People's Party is losing out.

But there a signs of a deeper malaise. "On the whole the coalition won't work much any more. Creditanstalt was a stumbling block and the next will follow," said Andreas Koller, political analyst at the Salzburger Nachrichten daily.
"They have diverging points of view on many points -- the media, the family, working hours and social policy," he said.

The two parties were also at loggerheads last year over Austrian neutrality. Vranitzky wants no change but the conservatives once again find themselves closer to Haider, who wants Austria to join NATO.
